#6372. A Common Meat Triggers a Unique Muscle-Building Peptide, Study Finds

A new study found that lean ground pork triggered a distinctive increase in a naturally occurring peptide linked to muscle growth.

A new study suggests that the way the body processes protein after exercise may depend on more than how much protein a meal contains. Researchers found that lean ground pork produced a distinctive increase in a naturally occurring peptide linked to muscle protein synthesis, the biological process responsible for building and repairing muscle proteins.

Published in Molecular Nutrition & Food Research, the research examined how different protein sources affect amino acids and peptides circulating in the bloodstream after resistance exercise. The findings suggest that the structure and composition of whole foods may influence how protein is digested and made available to the body.

Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign analyzed blood samples and muscle protein synthesis measurements from two randomized controlled trials involving healthy young adults.

Following resistance exercise, participants consumed one of five nutritional treatments: low-fat ground pork, high-fat ground pork, black beans and rice, an isolated nutrient beverage containing amino acids and other nutrients, or a carbohydrate-only control drink. Each protein-containing treatment supplied approximately 20 grams (0.7 ounces) of protein, allowing researchers to compare the body’s responses to different nutritional sources.

Among the five treatments, lean ground pork was the only one to produce a statistically significant increase above baseline in circulating dileucine, a peptide composed of two linked leucine molecules. Blood concentrations rose approximately 90 to 120 minutes after consumption. Dileucine has been associated with muscle protein synthesis, although scientists are still investigating its specific role in muscle metabolism.

Peak dileucine concentrations after lean ground pork consumption were significantly higher than those measured after the isolated nutrient beverage and carbohydrate control. However, the differences compared with high-fat ground pork and the beans-and-rice meal were not statistically significant.

Lean ground pork also produced the highest peak concentrations of leucine, an essential amino acid involved in regulating muscle protein synthesis. These levels were significantly higher than those following high-fat ground pork, beans and rice, or the carbohydrate control, but were not significantly different from the isolated nutrient beverage.

“These findings suggest that the body’s response to protein is influenced by more than the amount consumed,” said Nicholas A. Burd, PhD, corresponding author and researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. “Seeing how the whole-food matrix affects the release of amino acids and peptides into the bloodstream gives us a clearer picture of how dietary protein may actually drive muscle protein synthesis and remodeling.”

Across the protein-containing treatments, researchers identified a modest but statistically significant positive relationship between peak dileucine concentrations and changes in muscle protein synthesis. The same association was not observed with conventional leucine measurements.

Importantly, this does not establish that dileucine directly stimulates muscle growth or that lean ground pork produces greater muscle gains than other foods.

One possible explanation involves the food matrix, which encompasses a food’s physical structure and the interactions among its components. Researchers proposed that grinding meat could disrupt connective tissue, potentially making proteins more accessible to digestive enzymes and changing how amino acids and peptides enter the bloodstream.

The results add to research investigating how whole-food protein sources influence the body’s response to exercise. Although the protein content of a meal remains relevant, differences in food structure, fat content, and digestion may affect the timing and composition of nutrients reaching the bloodstream.

“Consumers often think about protein in terms of how many grams are on their plate, but science is showing us there is much more to the story,” said Kristen Hicks-Roof, PhD, RDN, LDN, Senior Director of Human Nutrition at the National Pork Board. “What’s exciting about this research is that it helps us better understand how a familiar food like ground pork delivers protein and how the body responds to it after exercise. Ground pork represents an important opportunity to connect emerging protein science with practical, nutritious meals people already enjoy.”

Further studies will be needed to determine whether these short-term biological responses translate into meaningful differences in muscle growth and recovery. Researchers also need to examine how dileucine behaves when protein sources are consumed as part of typical mixed meals and whether similar responses occur in older adults and other populations.

Reference: “Whole-Food Protein Sources Differentially Modulate Postprandial Plasma Dileucine Profiles in the Post-Exercise State” by Žan Zupančič, Geoffrey M. Provenzano, Calvin Chen, Gena L. Irwin, Alexander V. Ulanov and Nicholas A. Burd, 19 October 2026, Molecular Nutrition & Food Research. DOI: 10.1002/mnfr.70628

This study was supported by the National Pork Board.

#6371. Celebrating the Eater Awards Winners With a Party in NYC

Eater Awards celebrated the best restaurants, chefs, and more of 2026

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

What a night. On Sunday, November 15, the winners of the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, celebrated together at Nine Orchard in NYC. More than 200 chefs, restaurateurs, bartenders, and friends of Eater — many of whom traveled across the country to be there — partook in live portraiture, custom engraving, and, of course, plenty of food and drink.

Now in its 17th year, the Eater Awards recognize the year’s best new restaurants, bakeries, bars, dishes, and chefs in markets across the U.S.. More than 30 Eater staffers and contributors spent months traveling to 44 cities to weigh contenders on food, service, atmosphere, and the stories behind them. The prize? A tomato can trophy. And yes, they’re real.

The night started off strong with photos at the tomato can-wrapped step-and-repeat and a welcome shot of Zbiotics, before guests headed up to the roof of Nine Orchard for panoramic views and more fun. The party was filled with unique moments, from custom lighter engraving presented by Toast to live water color portraits presented by Capital One. Rounds of dishes inspired by the winning restaurants were passed.

A champagne toast commemorated the resiliency of the hospitality industry. “Thank you for what you do, every single day, to bolster your team, your community, and the restaurant industry at large,” said Eater editor in chief Stephanie Wu.

Rose Previte of DC’s Maydan, Medina, and Souk, and 2026 Best New Restaurant winner Maydan Market LA joined Wu on stage to present the first-ever Pre Shift Future of Hospitality Award to Maison Bar à Vins. This peer-voted award honors one winner whose work is particularly forward-thinking, challenges conventions, sets new standards, and points toward the future of hospitality. Matt Conroy and Jason Chavenson took home the surprise award.

“It’s really amazing to win an award like this that’s voted by everybody here and, you know, so many people we look up to, so it’s really incredible,” said Matt Conroy.

All attendees received an Eater tote filled with editor-curated products including Bubs candy, Zbiotics, TimeSavvy’s self-care and travel essentials kit, sweet matcha drops and fiery garlic chili sauce from Bokksu, a Wood Cabin candle from Keap Candles, chef socks from Cargo Crew, and a gift certificate for a pair of shoes from Snibbs.

It truly was a great night celebrating the hard work these chefs and their teams put into creating the best dining experiences of the year. Feeling FOMO? Check out the full list of winners and see for yourself what made these restaurants and chefs stand out.

#6370. Ultra-Thin "Rainbow" Sails Could Power Spacecraft and Shade the Earth

For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum, and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind âsolar sailingâ, which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed actually feasible. Now a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), has unveiled a clever technique that will allow these giant sails to steer sideways using a technology more commonly associated with flat-screen displays.

That technology is liquid crystals, most commonly used in liquid crystal displays (LCDs). Instead of having the sail itself act like a giant mirror and requiring it to angle itself in order to turn relative to the Sun, the sail described by the RIT researchers bends sunlight at a steep angle via diffraction, allowing the spacecraft to steer sideways while still facing directly at the Sun.

This solution offers several advantages over traditional solar sails. The best analogy to describe how is to think of holding an umbrella against a stiff breeze. If you hold the umbrella directly facing the direction of the wind, it will push you straight back â simple enough. But, if you want to âturnâ compared to the direction of the wind, you have to angle the umbrella. In so doing, you not only lower the total amount of wind hitting the umbrella, but also make it much harder to control.

Fraser talks about how critical folding of solar sails is to their operation.

Traditional solar sails face the exact same problem, only in space instead of in an atmosphere and with sunlight instead of wind. Nearly a decade ago, Grover Swartzlander Jr, one of the paperâs authors and a professor at RIT, realized that microscopic optical patterns that reflected light to the side would replace mechanical tilting in solar sails. To prove his point, he received backing from NASAâs Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) program, and laid out the groundwork for what became diffractive solar sails.

When light hits a diffraction grating, the technical term for the microscopic patterns embedded in the sail similar to what is etched onto a CD, it bounces off at steep, predictable angles even when the surface is facing the Sun head-on. Pushing the light to one side provides the sail with an equal and opposite kick in the other direction, steering the spacecraft using nothing more than a simple roll.

While much of the early work on diffractive sail prototypes focused on patterns etched into metal-coated films, they struggled with scaling and had a hard time rolling into a rocket fairing. Hence the turn to LCDs. The new study, where the RIT team -drawing on technical input from BEAM engineering and diffractive-sail researchers at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.

Fraser talks about how great solar sails are for travel in the solar system and beyond.

These flexible plastics contain rod-shaped molecules that naturally twist into microscopic spirals, creating layers of differing refractive indices that bend light using a phenomenon called the Pancharatnam phase. This is a way of bending or delaying light by twisting the direction the waves wiggle (its âpolarizationâ). Sails made out of this material have the added advantage of being lightweight, flexible, and easy to scale up manufacturing while still being able to fit inside a compact spacecraft.

Thereâs only one problem - a single liquid crystal layer only interacts with a very specific wavelength of light, allowing the rest to pass through unimpeded, and taking all their pushing power with them. To figure out how to solve this problem, the researchers turned to computer simulations, eventually using an optimization algorithm to design a three-layer sandwich of liquid crystals. The top layer catches blue and visible light, the middle layer grabs infrared, and the bottom layer interacts only with longer infrared rays. Even with those three separate layers, the combined film is only 5.5 micrometers thick, one-tenth the width of a human hair.

Such a setup would offer a major advantage in one potential use for a massive solar sail - as a âplanetary sunshadeâ. Scientists have long proposed parking a giant sheet in orbit at the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point to deflect a small fraction of the sunlight reaching the planet, in an effort to intentionally cool it. With traditional materials, such a shade would need to tilt in order to keep its position, consequently shrinking its shadow. But one made out of diffractive material could hold its position without compromising its size. And with the new chiral liquid crystal setup, if the middle layer is left out, the near-infrared wavelengths used by solar panels to generate electricity would still pass through - or the layers could be tuned to let the red light needed for plant photosynthesis pass through - while the rest of the sunlight still pushes on the sail.

Fraser talks about what a solar sail actually is.

All that being said, this concept is still at a very early stage. They havenât yet built a prototype of the three-layer system, let alone one that could stand the rigors of launch or the constant bombardment of the solar wind. But the paper offers a step to a potential solution to one of the most fundamental problems in solar sail design - and given the major advantages it has as a propulsion system, itâs only a matter of time before someone trials this new idea in the vacuum of space.

S. K. Sasanapur, X. Shan, & G. S. Swartzlander, Jr. - Optimized Bragg Grating Liquid Crystal Solar Sail

#6369. What 8 Cool Food People Outsource for Thanksgiving

﻿Laila Gohar, Deb Perelman, and others share their top tips

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

“There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World

“I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the big stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen

“We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash

“I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

“Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World

“We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya

#6368. SpaceX Dragon Returns to Earth With a Treasure Trove of Scientific Secrets

A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft has returned to Earth carrying an unusual collection of scientific cargo, including cancer research samples, 3D-printed blood vessels, and bacteria studied in space. The experiments could provide valuable insights into human health, lead to better medical treatments, and help astronauts stay healthy on future missions.

The uncrewed capsule splashed down in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles at 2:03 p.m. PST, successfully completing NASA’s 35th SpaceX commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station.

Dragon departed the orbiting laboratory at 11:05 a.m. CST on November 20, bringing back research materials that scientists can now examine in detail on Earth. Unlike many spacecraft that deliver supplies to the station, Dragon is also designed to return cargo safely, making it especially valuable for experiments that require further laboratory analysis.

Among the returning experiments is a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct created to investigate how blood vessels age and how cardiovascular diseases develop.

Bioprinting is a technology that uses living cells and specialized materials to build structures resembling human tissue. By studying these blood vessel models in microgravity, where objects experience near weightlessness, researchers hope to gain a better understanding of biological changes that may affect people both in space and on Earth.

Dragon also carried frozen tumor organoids that had undergone experimental treatments aboard the space station. Organoids are small, laboratory-grown models that reproduce certain characteristics of human tissues or tumors, allowing scientists to investigate diseases and test potential therapies.

Researchers hope these samples will reveal information that could improve cancer treatments and support personalized medicine, an approach that aims to tailor medical care to the characteristics of individual patients.

Another set of experiments focuses on antibiotic resistance, a growing medical concern worldwide. Frozen microbial samples returned aboard Dragon will help scientists examine how bacteria that resist antibiotic treatments survive, adapt, and evolve in the unusual environment of space.

Understanding these changes could be important for protecting astronauts on extended missions, when access to medical care is limited. The findings may also offer useful insights into how antibiotic-resistant microbes behave.

The returning cargo included a specialized lighting system that spent more than three years aboard the space station. Researchers used the equipment to investigate how lighting could improve astronauts’ sleep and overall well-being during long missions.

Light plays an important role in regulating the body’s internal clock, which influences when people feel alert or sleepy. Maintaining a healthy sleep schedule can be especially challenging aboard the space station, which circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes and experiences numerous sunrises and sunsets each day.

The spacecraft’s journey began on October 13, when it launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Dragon reached the International Space Station two days later, on October 15.

After spending more than a month at the orbiting laboratory, the spacecraft returned with scientific samples and equipment ready for further examination.

Although the experiments have not yet established new medical breakthroughs, the research could contribute to advances in cancer treatment, cardiovascular health, infectious disease research, and astronaut safety. The results may ultimately benefit patients on Earth while helping NASA prepare for longer journeys deeper into space.

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

Looking at these spaceflight return findings through the lens of keeping humans healthy in orbit, protecting a crew comes down to holding steady biological rhythms and physical resilience against constant environmental shifts in gravity, light cycles, radiation, thermal swings, and microbes—while looking at space as a continuous medium means there are also stresses we may not understand yet, and the real value of the returned cargo lies in the data it yields and how we can put those insights to use for crew health and protection. One useful way to picture that protection is a crystalline structured thread laid side by side and anchored into a sub-layer of material—clothing we wear in space travel over our vulnerable bodies without cross-weave bends: when the parallel alignment stays intact and locked into rotational closure (Ωπ) governed by π, it spreads mechanical, thermal, supplemental radiation, and even unfamiliar continuous-medium stress smoothly in a low-impedance regime (ΔZ → 0). Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds.

"Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg, an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS.

Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry.

Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. The occipital lobe houses the visual cortex, which helps process signals from the eyes. This area was relatively larger in Neanderthals than it is in modern humans.

In the new study, the researchers analyzed modern-human genomes for genetic variants that are related to occipital lobe size and were also likely inherited from Neanderthals. They discovered one such variant associated with the DAAM1 gene, which a 2019 study linked with brain development. This genetic variant was found only in modern humans outside Africa and was seen in five Neanderthal genomes.

Curiously, the Neanderthal variant the scientists detected in modern-human genomes led to an approximately 0.05-cubic-inch (0.85 cubic centimeters) reduction in occipital lobe size per copy of the variant in an individual. This means that the Neanderthal gene was linked to a slightly smaller brain size in modern humans.

A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk.

This effect is the opposite of what experts expected based on Neanderthals' large skull size, Tony Capra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, it's important to remember that this one gene variant "does not reflect the full set of variations that might have been present in Neanderthals that might have affected the shape and size of their brain structures," Capra noted.

Zeberg and Pääbo also discovered that having two copies of the DAAM1 gene variant was associated with a nearly 10% reduction in the chances of having schizophrenia in modern humans. But there was no apparent link between the variant and intelligence in modern humans.

"A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk," Zeberg said.

Symptoms of schizophrenia can include altered perceptions of reality, such as visual hallucinations and problems with processing visual signals. This makes it "tempting to speculate" that this Neanderthal gene variant's effects on schizophrenia might be associated with the visual cortex. However, there is currently no evidence for such a link, Zeberg said.

Future research along these lines could analyze how other Neanderthal genetic variants influenced modern humans, Capra said, "to see if they had a consistent effect on us." Looking into Neanderthal variants that are missing from modern-human genomes could "show us what makes us modern humans as opposed to them," Capra added.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Zeberg, H., & Pääbo, S. (2026). A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(48). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2624837123

#6366. Detecting Primordial Black Holes By The Stars They Destroy

Dark matter is hypothetical matter that makes up the large majority of the matter in the Universe, but we can't see it because it doesn't interact with light. Scientists put their minds into hyperdrive trying to understand it and figure out what it is. One of the proposals is that primordial black holes (PBH) account for some or all of dark matter.

Primordial black holes are hypothesized to have formed in the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang, from the direct collapse of pockets of dense matter. Really small PBHs wouldn't have survived this long because of Hawking Radiation, but more massive ones could have. New research focuses on asteroid-mass PBHs and how they could be detected, if they exist.

The research is "The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal. The lead author is Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT. The authors focus on what are called Hawking stars, stars that have engulfed a microscopic PBH. They're named after renowned physicist Stephen Hawking, who first proposed them in the 1970s.

"Primordial black holes (PBHs) in the asteroid mass window (1017â1023 g) remain viable dark matter candidates and can be captured by stars," the authors write. Though it's all theoretical at this point, the researchers developed a framework for what would happen to stars that capture these PBH. They used stellar evolution models, simulations, and other tools to try to understand what would happen.

Primordial Black Holes are only theoretical, so far. But if they exist, they could find their way inside main sequence stars. Image Credit: NASA and G. Bacon/STSCI

First of all, a single star on its own is unlikely to capture a PBH. But a star with a stellar or planetary companion would have enough gravitational interactions to trap a PBH in one of the stars. It could take thousands or even millions of year for a PBH to work its way into a star's center.

âThen, this is where the action begins,â said lead author Gottlieb. Once the PBH reaches the center, the star can't survive.

According to this work, there are two outcomes for stars that suffer this misfortune, and both spell doom. "We find that the fate of these systems bifurcates: PBHs that form an accretion disk before consuming the host drive explosive disruption, whereas PBHs captured too late or growing too slowly consume the star quietly," the authors write.

Once a PBH finds its way into the center of a star, it takes only a few million years before it consumes about 1% of the star's mass. Then, the rotation rate comes into play. If it's fast enough, the star's gas can't fall directly into the PBH. Instead, an accretion disk forms around the PBH, inside the star. This is where the two outcomes diverge.

âInside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,â Gottlieb said. This is an almost unimaginable scenario, but the research shows it's possible.

âThe black hole is also spinning, and itâs twisting space and time.â

The PBH then warps the star's magnetic fields, and just like in a SMBH, powerful jets are launched. âThis twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,â Gottlieb explains.

What star could survive powerful jets being emitted from inside?

âOnce the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,â said lead author Gottlieb. The authors write that this produces "an explosive Hawking-star transient powered by a rapidly spinning PBH." The PBH emits jets that tear through the star, quickly destroying it.

âAnd these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds," Gottlieb said. "Itâs very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.â

This schematic illustration shows the evolutionary sequence of a Hawking star. First the PBH is captured, and eventually it migrates into the stellar core. Once the PBH is embedded in the core, the PBH grows by accreting stellar mass. What happens next depends on whether the PBH forms a disk before it consumes its host. If a disk forms, that warps the magnetic fields, and the PBH launches jets from inside the star, destroying it in seconds. If no disk forms, the star dies a quiet, gradual death, and a stellar-mass black hole is left behind. Image Credit: Ore Gottlieb et al 2026 ApJ 1012 157

In the second case, the star's destruction is less cinematic. "The system dies quietly," the authors write, "leaving a PBH with mass of the order of the consumed stellar mass and little or no bright disk-powered emission." It's basically a stellar-mass black hole indistinguishable from others of its kind.

These two paths to destruction create different prospects for observing PBHs engulfed by stars.

"Our results carry important observational implications across both electromagnetic and GW channels," the authors explain. "If a PBH has grown sufficiently to form an accretion disk, the associated disk winds and relativistic jets can inject enough energy and momentum into the stellar envelope to unbind the star and power an explosive transient."

The rapid destruction creates a bright transient that emits EM radation across multiple wavelengths. This could be detectable at long distances with modern telescopes, similar to supernovae.

âWe would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,â Gottlieb says. âThis is something we could potentially detect, if itâs not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.â

This simulation depicts the moments after a primordial black hole is captured by a star. As soon as the black hole falls into the starâs center, it creates a swirling disk of material (orange). Within a matter of seconds, interactions between the black hole and the spinning disk should launch powerful jets of matter that ultimately pierce through the star, making it explode.

GWs from these events are likely more rare. Scientists have long wondered if PBH could be GW sources, and it's possible that the Hawking-star remnant that's left behind could be detected as one if it ever formed a compact binary with another compact object. The authors say that if this happens, it's exceedingly rare. But if it does happen, observing them would be very informative. "Thus, GW detections would be highly diagnostic if found, but should be regarded as a binary-evolution-limited and likely subdominant discovery channel for Hawking stars.

Here's where dark matter comes in. These Hawking-stars, if they exist and can be detected individually, could be used to calculate their population. If these stars work the way the researchers think they work, they can be detected and used to "provide independent observational constraints on the PBH population," the authors write. But on the other hand, "the absence of such transients or of convincing subsolar merger candidates could constrain the fraction of DM in PBHs."

So it seems there's a potential viable pathway to detect dark matter, if indeed PBHs are real and astronomers can find them destroying a star in a telltale blinding flash.

âThere is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,â Gottlieb said. âWe expect this to be visible, and itâs something we should look into.â

#6365. New Research Reveals Europa's Sodium Cloud Originated from its Interior Ocean

Jupiter's moon Europa has been fascinating astronomers and astrobiologists for decades. Ever since the Voyager probes passed through the system in 1979, scientists have theorized that an ocean lies beneath its icy crust. Further observations bolstered this theory, revealing surface plumes caused by warm water pushed up through vents in the crust (cryovolcanism). They've also found fascinating chemistry on the moon's surface, and an enormous, diffuse cloud of sodium surrounding it.

And now, observations by the W.K. Keck Observatory in Hawai'i have revealed something new and very surprising. That sodium cloud has remained remarkably stable after more than two decades of observations despite the dynamic and powerful forces that characterize Jupiter's environment. In a recent study led by Boston University, an interdisciplinary team of researchers compared sodium measurements high above Europa with observations of sodium clouds very close to the surface.

Their results, reported in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics, provide the first connection between the two, giving scientists a more complete view of the moon's environment. This, in turn, gives scientists a sneak peek at the ocean beneath Europa's surface. The team's observations relied on two decades of observations using Keck's High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HIRES) instrument, allowing them to map the sodium cloud's distribution and how it responds to changing conditions in the system.

Europa's sodium cloud is oblong-shaped, elongated in the east-west direction, and measures over 46,800 km (29,095 mi) in diameter, or about 30 times Europa's radius. Sodium is of particular interest to planetary scientists because it is a constituent of sodium chloride (salt), a key ingredient in Earth's oceans. Based on the latest fossil evidence, scientists theorize that life first emerged approximately 4 billion years ago in Earth's primordial oceans around hydrothermal vents.

Based on multiple lines of evidence, astrogeologists also believe that similar vents exist inside Europa at the core-mantle boundary. Understanding the origin and distribution of sodium around Europa can help researchers learn more about the materials on the moon's surface and potentially subsurface. Emma Lovett, a graduate student at Boston University and lead author on the study, explained in a W.M. Keck Observatory release:

We don't know a lot about Europa's hidden ocean and icy surface, but its atmosphere offers a window into this potentially habitable world. The whereabouts of life beyond Earth might be closer than we ever imagined.

However, studying sodium close to the moon's surface presents many challenges. Foremost among these is the highly reflective nature of Europa's surface ice, which can overwhelm the faint signal emitted by nearby gas. To overcome this problem, the team used the HIRES instrument's high-resolution, long-slit configuration to measure the sodium's distinctive spectral fingerprint. They also observed Europa as it passed through Jupiter's shadow, ensuring that there was no direct sunlight reflecting off the surface to interfere with the signals they detected.

By changing the instrument's orientation at multiple locations, the team mapped the sodium cloud rather than measuring its spectra at any single point. Lastly, they combined new observations with archival data Keck obtained in 1999 to see how the cloud changes over time. Surprisingly, they found that the cloud has remained stable despite changes in Jupiter's plasma environment and the influence of the neighboring volcanic moon Io, which spews sodium into space. Said Carl Schmidt, a researcher at Queen's University Belfast and Boston University:

The neighboring volcanic moon Io sprays sodium around the Jupiter system, and we've often wondered if Io paints Europa's surface. The stable sodium abundance in these Keck data shows that Europa is indifferent to Io's volcanic activity. What we observe originates in Europa's saltwater and not in Io's volcanoes.

Radiation from Jupiter can break apart molecules on Europa's surface. This can free oxygen, which could percolate in brines through the surface into the ocean under the ice. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

A particularly beneficial observation occured on September 29th, 2022, when NASA's Juno spacecraft passed behind the moon relative to the team's perspective. For the past ten years, Juno has studied Jupiter's atmosphere, magnetosphere, and plasma environment. So on this occasion, the team had the chance to study the sodium cloud alongside measurements of the local plasma cloud. This enabled the team to examine the sodium cloud across a range of conditions and to test the effects of Jupiter's magnetosphere and Io's volcanic activity.

While most astrobiology missions are currently searching for evidence for past life on Mars, Europa is the next target in the search for extraterrestrial life. Right now, NASA's Europa Clipper mission and the ESA's JUpiter ICy Moons Explorer (JUICE) are en route to the system to study this icy moon. Because Europa is not a terrestrial planet but an "Ocean World," it offers major opportunities to study potentially habitable environments beyond Earth. In particular, scientists want to see how water and other materials are transferred between the surface and the interior.

While no direct evidence of organic molecules has been detected on the surface, research strongly indicates the moon has the key chemical ingredients and pathways to form them. And while the sodium cloud does not provide a direct measurement of Europa's ocean, understanding its origin and behavior helps scientists understand the moon's chemical environment. Building on their momentum, the team is currently using the Hubble Space Telescope to look for magnesium in Europa's atmosphere, another possible element in Europa's ocean salts. As Lovett summarized:

These observations help us refine our models of Europa's atmosphere, testing what releases sodium and how radiation pressure shapes its distribution. We're also looking for magnesium, which has been tentatively detected on Europa's surface but not yet in its atmosphere. Finding it could provide another important clue to the salts present on this intriguing ocean world.

#6364. Ancient Meteorites May Have Delivered One of Life’s Most Essential Ingredients to Earth

Ancient meteorites may hold the key to understanding when and how Earth acquired one of life’s most essential elements.

Carbon erupting from Hawaiian volcanoes may have originated deep within Earth’s metallic core, carrying a chemical fingerprint that dates back to the planet’s formation. A new study suggests that carbon-rich meteorites delivered a substantial amount of Earth’s carbon during its early history, potentially helping supply the element that would eventually become essential to life.

Researchers analyzing volcanic rocks from Hawaii identified an unusual carbon isotope signature that may trace back to Earth’s core. “We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth’s core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface,” says lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor at Columbia University’s Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences and Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The researchers examined volcanic rocks from Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift, two Hawaiian volcanic systems that draw magma from different regions of the mantle. Samples from the Tantalus Rift contained carbon isotope signatures of approximately -5 to -7 per mil, consistent with typical mantle carbon. Kīlauea’s samples, however, had a much heavier signature of approximately -1 per mil, a value rarely observed in previous measurements.

“This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle,” says Moussallam. “This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core.” Although the team considers the core the most likely source, the isotope measurements do not establish that origin conclusively.

Earth’s mantle extends roughly 1,800 miles beneath the crust, separating the surface from the planet’s metallic core. Scientists believe much of Earth’s carbon resides in the core, which cannot be directly sampled. However, research suggests that some materials from the liquid outer core may cross into the mantle and eventually reach the surface through mantle plumes. These rising columns of hot rock can partially melt as they approach the crust, supplying magma to volcanoes. Kīlauea is thought to receive magma from near the center of a plume that originates close to the core-mantle boundary, while the Tantalus Rift samples appear to represent the plume’s outer regions.

To investigate the carbon carried by these magmas, Moussallam’s team used a recently developed technique to measure carbon isotopes inside tiny pockets of trapped melt. As magma cools, growing crystals can enclose droplets of molten rock before dissolved gases escape. These sealed pockets, called undegassed melt inclusions, preserve carbon dioxide from the original magma. “These melts are fossils of the magma,” Moussallam says.

The researchers then compared Kīlauea’s unusual carbon signature with measurements from ancient meteorites. Moussallam argues that carbon preserved in Earth’s core should reflect “the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created.” The closest similarities appeared in carbonaceous chondrites, a carbon-rich class of meteorites associated with the outer regions of the early solar system.

Chondrites contain some of the solar system’s oldest surviving material, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. “All of Earth is made of chondrites,” Moussallam explains. “They’re the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets.” Scientists distinguish between noncarbonaceous chondrites, associated with the inner solar system, and carbonaceous chondrites, which formed farther from the Sun. How much each group contributed to Earth’s formation remains debated.

The researchers propose that carbonaceous chondrites struck Earth relatively late in its formation, when the growing planet was better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have entered the core before eventually moving into the mantle and reaching the surface through volcanic activity. The isotope similarities support this possibility, but confirming that the carbon actually originated in the core will require additional evidence. “We don’t really know. We need more measurements,” cautions Moussallam.

The proposed journey would connect carbon delivered by ancient meteorites, stored deep inside Earth, and eventually released into the environment where living organisms could incorporate it. “It’s fun to think about. We’re made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet’s core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting.”

Reference: “Isotopically heavy carbon in the core” by Yves Moussallam, Damanveer S. Grewal, Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, Estelle F. Rose-Koga, Allan Lerner, Bridgett Holman, Paul J. Wallace, Natália Gauer Pasqualon, Olivia E. Anderson and Matthew G. Jackson, 9 November 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2610912123

#6363. Amazon’s New 6-Inch Kindle Is So Small, I Bring Mine Everywhere

This tiny e-reader is fast, cute, and built for commuting.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Amazon just gave its Kindle lineup a major makeover, and the smallest model might be the most exciting. Earlier this month, the company introduced a redesigned 6-inch Kindle that's more compact than any e-reader users have seen before. It’s got a sleek new look, faster performance, and four gorgeous colors that make the popular device feel like a cute accessory in its own right. After spending some time with the new Alpine Sky version, I can confidently say that its tiny size is one of my favorite things about it.

The new Kindle is officially Amazon's most pocket-sized e-reader yet, featuring a redesigned flush-front display that eliminates the raised border around the screen. The 6-inch, 300-ppi glare-free display is still black and white, but the device itself now has color that stretches seamlessly from front to back. Amazon also says the new Kindle opens books 30 percent faster than its predecessor and offers up to six weeks of battery life on a single charge, which has been ideal for me, someone who forgets to charge any of his devices.

One of the biggest updates is the introduction of two different versions of the 6-inch Kindle. The standard model starts at $149.99 and comes in Ube (a pretty purple shade) and classic Graphite, with 16 GB of storage. For $189.99, you can upgrade to the new Kindle Aluminum, which comes in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green, with a premium matte aluminum back, 32GB of storage, and no lock-screen ads.

I have the Alpine Sky version, which has a beautiful, soft blue finish that always gets compliments from friends. But beyond the new colors and materials, I've appreciated most how easy this little thing is to bring everywhere. I live in New York City, so I'm constantly taking the subway, and carrying a physical book around isn't always convenient. It’s not impossible, but it can be a nuisance when I'm reading something particularly thick. The Kindle is smaller than most of the books I own, takes up little room in my bag, and feels comfortable to hold for longer reading sessions without making my hand ache.

I also love that I can throw it into pretty much any bag I'm carrying, whether it's a small everyday bag or something much larger. And, admittedly, there's something funny about watching other commuters on the subway notice it. I swear I can see people clocking the tiny blue Kindle and thinking how cute it is (but that could just be my main-character energy). The text is still plenty readable despite its smaller display, and sometimes I feel like the person sitting next to me is following along with whatever chapter I'm on.

Of course, the smaller Kindle doesn't have every feature you'll find on Amazon's pricier models. It lacks waterproofing and adjustable warm lighting like the Kindle Paperwhite, so readers who prioritize those features may prefer the larger option. But if you want a convenient, portable way to read, there's plenty to appreciate here.

The new 6-inch Kindle and Kindle Aluminum are available to shop now, with prices starting at $149.99. Whether you're new to e-reading or just want something smaller for your commute, Amazon's latest release makes a pretty convincing case for carrying an entire library in your bag.

#6362. Earth’s Ozone Hole Swells to More Than Twice the Size of the United States

An unusually powerful polar vortex caused the Antarctic ozone hole to swell to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, covering more than twice the area of the United States.

Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, making it one of the largest observed in nearly five decades. Despite its extraordinary size, scientists from NASA and NOAA emphasize that Earth’s protective ozone layer continues to recover and remains on course to heal later this century.

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a powerful circulation of winds surrounding Antarctica. However, they also noted that decades of international efforts to reduce ozone-destroying chemicals prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

Between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was most intense, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone high in the atmosphere because it serves as Earth’s natural “sunscreen,” protecting living organisms from harmful ultraviolet radiation. This beneficial ozone in the stratosphere differs from ground level ozone, an air pollutant often produced by human activities.

“The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.”

The ozone hole reached its maximum size on September 18, expanding to 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). That was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

“The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” Newman said.

Ozone destruction begins with human-made chemicals containing chlorine and bromine. After entering the environment, these compounds gradually rise into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet sunlight breaks them apart and releases chlorine and bromine atoms. These atoms can then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in clouds that form in the extremely cold Antarctic stratosphere, leading to the breakdown of ozone.

A major factor in this process is the polar vortex, a seasonal ring of strong winds that circulates around Antarctica high in the atmosphere. By trapping exceptionally cold air over the continent, the vortex creates conditions that allow polar stratospheric clouds to develop. These clouds provide an important environment for the chemical reactions responsible for ozone depletion.

In 2026, the polar vortex was unusually extensive because atmospheric disturbances that normally weaken and disrupt it were less active than usual.

“The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. “That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.”

Although the 2026 ozone hole covered an exceptionally large area, the amount of ozone lost within it was less severe than during some of the most extreme depletion events recorded over the previous 10 to 20 years.

To measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers used instruments carried into the atmosphere by balloons launched from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected measurements with the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical instrument designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations showed that ozone directly above the South Pole fell to its lowest concentration of the year on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

A Dobson unit is a standard measurement used to describe the total amount of ozone in a vertical column of the atmosphere. For comparison, 100 Dobson units would form a layer just 1 millimeter thick, roughly the thickness of a dime, if all the ozone were compressed to standard temperature and pressure at sea level. The lowest concentration ever measured above the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.

Satellites have provided another essential source of ozone measurements since 1979. For the 2026 assessment, scientists drew on observations from instruments aboard NASA’s Aura satellite, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, a mission operated jointly by NASA and NOAA. Together, these observations help researchers track changes in ozone levels and assess the atmosphere’s recovery over time.

Despite the unusually large ozone hole in 2026, long-term measurements continue to demonstrate the benefits of international action to protect the atmosphere. NASA and NOAA scientists point to the Montreal Protocol, adopted in 1987, as a major reason the ozone layer is gradually recovering.

Under the agreement, countries committed to phasing out substances that damage ozone, including chlorofluorocarbons, and replacing them with alternatives that pose less risk to the ozone layer. These restrictions have substantially reduced the amount of ozone-destroying chemicals entering the atmosphere.

According to Stephen Montzka, a senior scientist at NOAA’s Global Monitoring Laboratory, chlorine concentrations in the Antarctic stratosphere associated with ozone-depleting substances have fallen by approximately one-third from their peak levels in the 1980s. This decline has helped reduce the severity of ozone destruction, even during years when atmospheric conditions favor the formation of a particularly large hole.

Chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once common ingredients in products and materials used around the world, including refrigerators, air conditioners, and building insulation.

Although many of these chemicals have been phased out, their effects persist. Some remain in the atmosphere for decades, while others continue to escape from aging equipment, discarded products, and landfills. As a result, ozone recovery is a gradual process that depends on the continued decline of these long-lasting pollutants.

Scientists currently estimate that the Antarctic ozone hole will recover by the 2070s as the remaining ozone-destroying substances slowly disappear from the atmosphere. The enormous hole observed in 2026 demonstrates how strongly unusual weather can influence ozone depletion from one year to the next. At the same time, its reduced severity compared with the worst years on record provides further evidence that international efforts to protect Earth’s ozone layer are making a lasting difference.

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

“Despite its extraordinary size, scientists from NASA and NOAA emphasize that Earth’s protective ozone layer continues to recover and remains on course to heal later this century.”

This claim is like whistling in the dark. If one examines the historical records, it is obvious that the effect of the Antarctic circumpolar vortex on ozone extent and concentration is more highly correlated with the strength of the vortex (and hence temperatures) than the concentration of stratospheric halides, which don’t change much from year to year. Just as very strong circumpolar vortexes produce large ‘ozone holes,’ weak vortexes, or ones that break up early, result in anomalously small ‘holes.’

The recent ‘holes’ are indistinguishable from what was seen during the 1990s, shortly after the passage of the Montreal Protocol.

Perhaps more to the point, the real concern is (or should be) the effect of low ozone concentrations on the surface UV flux because of the potential biological impacts. What is never mentioned by those who make their living from monitoring the ‘ozone holes, is that the sun is NEVER directly above the ‘ozone hole.’ The sun’s rays come in obliquely, with a long slant-range, while the sun is close to the horizon. Also, there is usually an enhanced concentration of ozone outside the vortex, created by the Brewer-Dobson circulation moving tropical stratospheric ozone to Antarctica, as seen here: https://scitechdaily.com/antarctic-ozone-hole-is-the-smallest-on-record-since-its-discovery/ This results in strong absorption of the UV before it even gets near the ‘hole.’ The public is only given a highly biased description of what is happening.

NASA Ozone Watch, with historical data, is not currently available with no explanation given.

“However, they also noted that decades of international efforts to reduce ozone-destroying chemicals prevented the hole from becoming even larger.”

This assertion is speculation. Where is the graph and maps showing the decline in Antarctic halides?

“…, where ultraviolet sunlight breaks them apart and releases chlorine and bromine atoms.”

Ozone, O3, is a very unstable molecule. Most break down within an hour or two. None last more than 24 hrs. Ergo, the whole ozone layer recovers daily.

There is a little more to it than that. Most of Earth’s ozone is produced in the tropical stratosphere. It is moved polewards by the Brewer-Dobson circulation. For most of the year, decayed-ozone (oxygen) over Antarctica is replaced with fresh ozone from the tropics. However, once the Winter circumpolar vortex sets up, the new ozone can’t get passed the outer edge of the vortex and builds up outside instead of moving into the interior; that ozone destruction briefly accelerates in the early-Spring, when the sun’s rays first start to arrive past the Antarctic Circle, because of photo-catalytic destruction driven by extremely cold temperatures. When the vortex breaks up in mid-October, the anomalously-high ozone concentration outside the vortex again moves into the interior of the Antarctic Circle and re-establishes the typical ozone concentration.

#6361. Making Sense of Chaotic Supernova Ejecta With the JWST

Finding order in the chaotic aftermath of a supernova explosion isn't easy. But the JWST has the tools to do it. Its Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) and its Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) were built for situations like this.

Massive stars play an important role in the evolution of the cosmos. They're responsible for synthesizing astronomical metals, the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium that are necessary to form everything from rocky planets to living organisms. Without massive stars, the cosmos would look much different. It would be a simple mixture of hydrogen, with a little helium mixed in, and trace amounts of lithium. Nature can't build planets or create life with that limited palette.

Astrophysicists can't see inside stars to learn more about this process, so they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out and then examine the results.

Massive stars live fast and die young, then explode as supernovae. When that happens, the explosion sends their contents, including their astronomical metals, out into the interstellar medium. Once there, it's available not only for planets and life, but for the next generation of stars.

When a supernova explodes, it leaves behind a supernova remnant, the matter ejected by the explosion in an expanding shockwave. The shockwave heats up the expanding shell, creating some of Nature's most stunning displays. The shocks can also rebound, creating an inward shock wave. It can create a real mess, but there are still patterns to be discerned. Within the exanding shell, molecules come form that tell astrophysicists what happened inside the star prior to its explosion.

One of the most well-known supernova remnants is Cassiopeia A (Cas A). It's about 11,000 light years away, and it was observed by Earthlings around 1667. Astronomers are interested in it because they can learn a lot about the exploding star that created itâthe progenitorâby analyzing its contents.

The JWST was built for just such an endeavour. In new research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, a team of researchers used the JWST's MIRI and MRS to determine Cas A's chemical makeup. The research is "JWST Resolves Dust Emission from Individual Ejecta Clumps in Cassiopeia A: Dominant Grain Compositions Point to a Shell Merger in the Progenitor," and the lead author is Tea Temim, a research scientist from Columbia University.

"We present a study of dust emission in the supernova remnant (SNR) Cassiopeia A (Cas A) observed with the MIRI Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) on board JWST," the authors write. "The unprecedented spatial resolution at mid-IR wavelengths allows us to isolate dust emission from individual arcsecond-scale clumps of supernova (SN) ejecta and circumstellar material (CSM) and identify the dominant dust species in each chemically distinct region."

Massive stars fuse different elements in layers, and that's reflected in the remnants they leave behind when they explode. Increasingly heavier elements are forged in the core, up until iron is reached. Lighter elements are fused together in the surrounding layers. These layers tell the star's history, but it all gets blown into space when the star explodes as a supernovae. To make matters more complicated, these shock waves can bounce back as reverse shocks.

The clumps in the supernova ejecta that the authors refer to are huge, as large as our Solar System. In studying these clumps with the MRS, the researchers were able to identify different dust species region by region, rather than as one mixed up jumble of spectra. They learned that the progenitor star underwent a shell merger.

âMaterial within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,â lead author Temim said in a press release. âSo, for example, this would be something like the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merging together and changing the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.â

Before they turned to the JWST, they used Spitzer images to identify regions to focus on with the JWST.

This figure shows Spitzer images on the left and JWST images on the right. The JWST obviously has a much higher resolution, and the researchers used it to map Cas A's dust chemistry all across the remnant. The observations led to a better understanding of the shell mergers the remnant went through right before it exploded, and a better understanding of the progenitor's overall structure. Since astrophysicists can't see inside stars, they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, JPL-Caltech, T. Temim (Columbia University), R. Arendt (UMBC), D. Milisavljevic (Purdue University). Image Processing: A. Pagan (STScI).

The Spitzer identified regions with different dust properties. The researchers focused on three of them with MRS.

"The MRS spectra extracted at positions P1, P2, and P3 ... all exhibit significant emission from warm dust, but with spectral shapes that differ considerably between the three regions," the authors write.

This image shows the overall supernova remnant and the locations of three regions with distinctly different dust properties first identified with the Spitzer Space Telescope. The researchers examined these regions more closely with the JWST's MRS, seen as P1, P2 and P3. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Danny Milisavljevic (Purdue University), Tea Temim (Princeton University), Ilse De Looze (UGhent); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI).

P1 samples reverse-shocked ejecta that has bright argon emissions dominate by grains of SiO2 (silica). It helps the researchers track the outer layers of the supernova's ejecta. Finding it supports the idea that the progenitor underwent a carbonâoxygen shell merger.

P2 is centered on what astronomers call Cas A's "Green Monster" structure, which is the green structure near the center. It's emissions are attributed to circumstellar matter emissions on Cas A's near side, not material from Cas A's progenitor. It's likely made of mostly Mg2SiO4, which helps astronomers determine that the progenitor's dust and the CSM dust are distinct from one another.

P3 is another reverse-shocked region. It has very bright neon emissions compared to P1. That favours another shell merger, this time between a carbon shell and an oxygen shell.

This image of Cas A is from the JWST's MIRI F2100W filter. The P1, P2, and P3 regions are indicated by the white arrows. "The spatial distribution of the P2-like emission associated with Mg2SiO4 CSM dust is shown in green, P1-like emission associated with SiO2 dust is shown in magenta, and P3-like Ne-rich emission associated with carbon dust is shown in blue," the authors write. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

"Identifying the different types of dust grains formed in the chemically distinct layers of a supernova brings us one step closer to understanding how much dust supernovae contribute to the interstellar dust reservoir in our galaxy," said co-author Ilse De Looze, associate professor at Ghent University in Belgium. "By revealing the composition of this newly formed supernova dust, JWST also provides crucial insights into how well these grains can survive the powerful reverse shocks that sweep through the supernova debris, ultimately determining how much dust can escape into the interstellar medium."

This JWST image of Cas A has the synchrotron emissions subtracted. Since synchrotron emissions are non-thermal, and since their emission lines overlap the lines from thermal dust, removing them helps to isolate the signal from the ejecta, which is what the researchers are interested in. So this image basically tracks the thermal emissions from carbon dust. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

The JWST played a leading role in this effort to piece together what happened to Cas A's progenitor. But it's observations added to an existing observational base from JAXA's XRISM x-ray satellite and NASA's own Chandra X-ray Observatory. Taken together, the more complete picture shows that the progenitor's shell mergers were underway prior to its explosion as a supernova.

After all the imaging, processing, and fitting to models, this is the overall result. This figure shows which parts of the Cas A ejecta are from the existing circumstellar medium (left: Mg2SiO4 grains) and which parts are actually form the progenitor star (right: SiO2 grains.) Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

âWith Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,â said Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in the United States. âAs a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. Itâs telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.â

These results will also help build better model for understanding other supernova remnants.

The authors say this work shows how important the JWST's high-resolution images are for understanding dust ejecta in supernova remnants and how it was formed. (But smart Universe Today readers already know how important the JWST is.)

"It also demonstrates that spatially resolved dust compositions in young SNRs can serve as a powerful probe of the chemical structure and explosion properties of core-collapse SNe," they conclude.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."
